keep: Don't reorganise. Lower the cost of specifying and verifying the work, and the boundary moves itself.
title: Why Firms Exist
claim: If markets allocate so well, why is your company not a market? Coase asked at 21.
lede: Economics spent a century explaining why markets allocate resources efficiently without noticing that inside every firm, markets have been abolished and replaced by orders.
copy: Coase's question in 1937 is embarrassingly simple. If the price mechanism is the efficient way to coordinate production, why does anyone employ anybody? Why not contract for every task, every hour, in an open market? The answer is that using the market is not free. There are costs to discovering prices, negotiating terms, writing contracts, keeping secrets and enforcing agreements — and when those transaction costs exceed the cost of just telling someone what to do, you get a firm. The boundary of the firm sits exactly where those two costs cross.

Coase later called it “little more than an undergraduate essay”. Thirty-five years after publication he had already found the better line for its fate: “an article much cited and little used.” Fifty-four years after it, the paper was cited in his Nobel. Oliver Williamson turned transaction costs into an operational theory of governance — why you buy some inputs and make others, especially when an asset is specific to one relationship and therefore hostage to it. Hart and Holmström then asked what a contract can and can't specify, and what happens to the residual.

The practical version is the most useful org-design tool I know. Every make-or-buy decision, every outsourcing debate, every argument about whether to hire a contractor or an employee, is a transaction-cost calculation wearing a business-strategy costume. And the answer moves: anything that lowers the cost of contracting — standardised interfaces, escrow, reputation systems, cheap search — pushes the boundary toward the market and shrinks firms.

Which is why the theory keeps predicting things. Containerisation and standardised parts lowered the cost of buying rather than making, and supply chains disaggregated across borders. Marketplaces lowered search and enforcement costs, and whole categories of employment turned into contracting. If software keeps eating the cost of specifying and monitoring work, Coase says the firm keeps shrinking — and the interesting question is which costs stubbornly refuse to fall.

timeline.t: Coase, 20, an undergraduate on a travelling scholarship, visits American factories to study how industries are organised. He has his answer by the summer of 1932.
'The Nature of the Firm' appears in Economica. In 1972 Coase calls it “much cited and little used.”
Coase's 'The Problem of Social Cost' does the same trick to externalities.
Williamson builds transaction-cost economics into an operational theory of governance.
Coase receives the Nobel, more than fifty years after the essay.
Hart and Holmström win for contract theory — the incomplete-contracts descendant.

figures.d: Took the question on a study trip, had the answer at 21, and waited more than fifty years for anyone to build on it.
Turned an insight into a method: asset specificity, hold-up, and when to bring it in-house.
Worked out what happens when a contract can't specify everything — which is always.

contested: The strongest objection comes from inside the lineage. Holmström — a 2016 laureate for the theory's descendant — and Roberts, in 'The Boundaries of the Firm Revisited' (Journal of Economic Perspectives, 1998), found that transaction-cost and property-rights theories "are quite distinct in their empirical predictions, but neither offers a satisfactory account of a large variety of observed practices." The complaint is not that Coase asked the wrong question. It is that the theories built on his answer explain hold-up well and much of what firms actually do badly. Transaction costs also resist measurement, which makes the theory easier to apply after the fact than to test in advance — the gap Williamson, by his own account in his Nobel lecture, set out to close by turning Coase into a predictive theory that could be tested.
changed: I used to think of company structure as culture and preference. It's mostly a cost calculation, and the calculation is knowable. The corollary I didn't expect: if you want a smaller org, don't reorganise — go lower the cost of specifying and verifying the work, and the boundary moves on its own.

reading.why: About twenty pages, no mathematics, and it reframes an entire field.
For the lineage: Williamson, Hart, Holmström, and who won what.
Where the theory becomes usable: asset specificity and the hold-up problem.
Not about Coase at all, and the best practical companion to thinking about org boundaries.
